title: Checkout Test Recap
topic: A pooled average that points the wrong way
blurb: The product analyst dropped this A/B recap in the team channel.
prompt: An AI product analyst just shared this checkout-test recap. If two lines jump too far, tap them.

segments.label: On phones
segments.text: On mobile, the new checkout (B) beat the old one (A): 12% conversion vs 10%.

segments.label: On laptops
segments.text: On desktop, B also beat A: 32% conversion vs 30%.

segments.label: The messy split
segments.text: A routing bug sent 80% of A's visitors to desktop, while 80% of B's visitors landed on mobile, so the pooled averages come out 26% for A and 16% for B.

segments.label: The call
segments.text: Because A's combined conversion is 10 points higher (26% vs 16%), shipping the old checkout A to everyone will increase conversions.

segments.label: The VIP kicker
segments.text: On top of that, A hit 100% conversion with VIPs (2 purchases out of 2 visitors), proving VIPs strongly prefer the old page.

conclusion: AI verdict: Ship old checkout A everywhere — it leads overall (26% vs 16%) and has 100% VIP conversion.

flaws.original: B actually wins on both mobile and desktop. A's higher combined average is an artifact of A getting most of the high-converting desktop traffic.
flaws.corrupted: Because A's combined conversion is 10 points higher (26% vs 16%), shipping the old checkout A to everyone will increase conversions.

diagnosis_choices.label: A only looks better overall because it got almost all the high-converting desktop traffic. B actually beats A on every device.
You cannot compare conversion rates between mobile and desktop users at all.
26% minus 16% is a 62.5-point gap, not a 10-point gap.

fix_choices.label: Compare like with like (or re-run with a fair traffic split): B wins on both mobile and desktop, so B is the better page.
Ignore the device breakdown, because the combined average always overrides the subgroups.
Ship A on desktop and A on mobile to lock in that 26% overall rate.

flaws.explanation: Desktop already converts about 3× better than mobile. Giving the old page mostly desktop traffic inflates its pooled average, even though the new page beats it on both mobile (12% > 10%) and desktop (32% > 30%).
flaws.why_tempting: The big combined number (26% vs 16%) feels more 'official' than the device breakdown — until you look at who was sent where.
flaws.catch_rule: When a combined average contradicts every subgroup, check whether the groups were mixed in very different proportions.
flaws.hint: If B won on phones and won on laptops, how did A end up with the better overall rate?

practice.problem: A new tutoring app beats the old one in every city, but the old app still has a higher overall pass rate. How is that possible?
practice.answer: The old app was mostly used in cities that already had high pass rates, so its combined average looks better even though it loses everywhere you compare fairly.

flaws.original: With only 2 VIP visitors, 2-for-2 is just a coin flip — far too little data to claim VIPs prefer A.
flaws.corrupted: On top of that, A hit 100% conversion with VIPs (2 purchases out of 2 visitors), proving VIPs strongly prefer the old page.

diagnosis_choices.label: 2 out of 2 visitors is just noise. That '100%' proves nothing about what VIPs prefer.
A 100% conversion rate is mathematically impossible in an A/B test.
VIP users should never be included in a checkout experiment.

fix_choices.label: Treat n = 2 as inconclusive and collect a much larger, randomized VIP sample before making a call.
Report it as 'nearly 100%' (say 95%) so it sounds more conservative.
Drop one of the two VIP visitors to reduce variance.

flaws.explanation: A headline '100%' can hide a denominator of 2. A fair coin comes up heads twice in a row 25% of the time — two lucky visitors prove nothing.
flaws.why_tempting: Extreme percentages like '100%' sound decisive, especially when the tiny count is tucked into parentheses.
flaws.catch_rule: Whenever you see an eye-popping percentage, immediately check the raw count behind it.
flaws.hint: Look at the numbers in parentheses after that 100%.

practice.problem: A new cafe has 5.0 stars from 2 reviews; the place next door has 4.7 stars from 1,400 reviews. Why isn't 5.0 the obvious winner?
practice.answer: With only 2 reviews, 5.0 can be two friends or two lucky nights — the number is too shaky to trust.

clean_segments: On mobile, the new checkout (B) beat the old one (A): 12% vs 10%.
On desktop, B also beat A: 32% vs 30%.
A routing bug sent 80% desktop traffic to A and 80% mobile traffic to B, which distorts the pooled averages (26% vs 16%).
Because B wins on every device, A's overall lead is an artifact of the traffic mix; fix the split or ship B.
The VIP '100%' is 2 out of 2 visitors — far too small to support any claim.
clean_conclusion: The new page wins on both phones and laptops. Don't ship the old one just because a broken traffic split padded its average.

diagnosis: The 10% mobile rate is higher than 12%.
The mobile rates belong to desktop traffic.
A two-point gap means mobile B converted twice as often as A.
fix: Move the 12% vs 10% figures to desktop.
Rewrite 12% as twice 10% when comparing mobile.

diagnosis: A outperformed B on desktop because 30 is the smaller rate.
The desktop lift was 20 percentage points.
The desktop rate for B must be taken from mobile instead.
fix: Give the desktop win to A.

diagnosis: A should weight mobile at 80% because B had that mix.
The pooled rates must average desktop and mobile equally.
Both versions should report their desktop rates as overall rates.
fix: Compute A with 80% mobile and 20% desktop.
Use 20% overall for A and 22% for B.
Use 30% overall for A and 32% for B.
